source_text: Nos vero renasci omnes Baptismate debere, et opere nostro et sermone testamur; sed non ut huius impertitione beneficii, de iure videantur diaboli plagiati; verum ut qui sunt opera Dei, fiant pignora Dei; et qui nascuntur viliter, non tamen noxie, renascantur pretiose, non tamen calumniose; quique prodeunt ex institutis Dei, provehantur mysteriis Dei; et qui afferunt opera naturae, dona gratiae consequantur; ac Dominus suus qui eos fecit condendo bonos, faciat innovando adoptandoque meliores. Ergo iure dicitur, confitearis necesse est, naturale quod Manichaeus finxerat, sed tu nomine commutato originale vocas, interiisse peccatum. Nec hoc ea catholica fides credit antiquitus, quae non dubitat et parvulos a Deo fieri, et malum ab eo nihil fieri: ac per hoc opera Dei ante liberae voluntatis usum, naturae praeiudicio nec rea, nec sub diaboli iure constituit.
pass_a_gloss: But we testify both by our work and by speech that all ought to be reborn by Baptism; but not so that by the imparting of this benefit they may seem plagiarized from the devil's right; but so that those who are works of God may become pledges of God; and those who are born cheaply, not nevertheless harmfully, may be reborn preciously, not nevertheless calumniously; and those who come forth from God's institutions may be advanced by God's mysteries; and those who bring the works of nature may obtain the gifts of grace; and their Lord who made them good by founding may make them better by renewing and adopting. Therefore it is rightly said, you must confess, that the natural which Manichaeus had feigned, but you with the name changed call original, has perished as sin. Nor does that ancient catholic faith believe this, which does not doubt both that little ones are made by God, and that no evil is made by him: and through this it does not establish the works of God before the use of free will as guilty by a prior judgment of nature, nor under the devil's right.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
Blaise originalis; Julian's mali originalis, not a later system slogan
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: By both our practice and our speech, we testify that everyone must be reborn through baptism. But this benefit is not bestowed so that people seem to have been kidnapped from the devil’s rightful possession. Rather, those who are God’s works become God’s children; those born in a lowly condition, but not a guilty one, are reborn at great worth, but without a false accusation. Those who come forth from God’s institutions are advanced by God’s mysteries; those who bring nature’s works receive grace’s gifts. Their Lord, who made them good by creating them, makes them better by renewing and adopting them. You must therefore confess that it is rightly said that the natural sin Mani invented, which you call original sin with a change of name, has perished. Nor does the catholic faith handed down from ancient times believe it: that faith does not doubt that infants are made by God and that nothing evil is made by him. Consequently, it does not pronounce God’s works guilty or place them under the devil’s jurisdiction, through a prejudgment against nature, before they exercise free will.

choices.why: Julian names the opinion of original evil (mali originalis) as what Rom 5:12's 'one man' crushed; keep his phrase, not a later original-sin system.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
